content:
Your church can face claims involving injuries, damaged property or leadership decisions. Insurance offers different kinds of protection for those risks. Start by asking what your church actually needs covered.

Use this reference to prepare for a conversation with a licensed insurance agent or broker. Ask them to connect each recommendation to your ministry activities and the terms of the proposed policy.

---

## Describe the ministry before requesting a quote

Give the agent a written picture of your operations. Include meeting locations, equipment, paid workers and volunteer activities. Describe children's programs, transportation and any space you rent. Ask which activities need separate coverage or an endorsement.

If you already have insurance, provide the current policy for review. Ask the agent to identify gaps and overlapping coverage. If a sending church or network arranges insurance, ask whose organization and activities the policy covers, including your plant's.

---

## Match coverage to the risk

Use these categories as a discussion list. Ask which protections appear in the proposal and which require additions.

| Coverage | What to discuss |
|---|---|
| General liability | Claims that your operations injured someone or damaged someone else's property, plus defense of covered claims. |
| Property | Buildings and belongings, including furniture and equipment, against covered damage or loss. |
| Management liability, including directors and officers | Claims arising from leadership decisions, including protection for the organization and its leaders. |
| Employment practices liability | Employee allegations of discrimination, harassment or wrongful dismissal. |
| Crime | Theft, fraud and employee dishonesty. |
| Cyber liability | Financial losses and liabilities involving data breaches or cyberattacks. |
| Umbrella liability | Additional liability protection above the limits of underlying policies. |

General liability can address injury and property-damage claims from your premises or operations. Ask about legal defense as well as damages. For an umbrella proposal, ask which underlying policies it extends and which risks remain excluded.

---

## Read the venue agreement with your agent

Do not assume the landlord's insurance protects the church's belongings. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners warns tenants to check their own property coverage and read their leases carefully.

Give your agent the venue's insurance requirements. Ask a local attorney to review the agreement's liability obligations. Confirm who must provide a certificate of insurance, whether the venue must be an additional insured, and what policy terms would provide that status.

<Callout type="warning">
A certificate of insurance summarizes coverage. It does not expand the policy. Ask the agent to verify the actual coverage supporting any additional-insured request.
</Callout>

Check that the agreement describes the rooms, access times and intended activities accurately. Include setup and teardown when describing how you will use the space. Ask about the church's liability for damage to property in its care.

---

## Follow equipment and vehicles beyond the venue

Property questions should follow your equipment wherever you use or store it. Describe instruments, sound equipment and computers, including items kept away from your meeting location. Ask about inland marine coverage for movable equipment in transit or temporarily off-site.

Document the assets and keep purchase records and photographs. Ask the agent how to value the equipment for the proposed coverage, including whether payment would reflect replacement cost or depreciation.

<Callout type="tip">
Walk the agent through an equipment move. Where is it stored, how does it travel, and where is it used? Ask them to identify coverage for each part of that trip.
</Callout>

Discuss vehicles separately. Hired and non-owned auto liability addresses organizational risks when workers or volunteers drive personal vehicles for ministry or the church rents a vehicle. Ask separately about damage to a rented vehicle itself and about any church-owned vehicles.

---

## Ask explicitly about abuse coverage

Sexual misconduct and molestation liability is a specialized coverage category. Ask about allegations involving the church, employees and volunteers. Have the agent explain who is insured, the covered allegations, exclusions and the available legal defense.

Ask them to identify the relevant policy wording rather than relying on a general description of church liability insurance. Coverage details vary. Ask whether the insurer requires or offers abuse-prevention measures, and discuss them alongside the coverage review.

Keep the discussion about insurance specific. Ask what the proposed policy requires of your church and how to report an allegation to the insurer.

---

## Check workers' compensation with your state

Ask your state's workers' compensation agency how its requirements apply to your church and each worker's duties. Do not decide that every worker is exempt because the employer is religious.

For example, New York's Workers' Compensation Board lists a nonprofit exception for clergy and religious-order members whose work consists solely of religious duties. Ask the Board about the actual duties before relying on that exception. Treat this as a New York example, not a rule for another state.

<Callout type="important">
State requirements and policy offerings can change. Confirm current requirements with your state's workers' compensation agency and confirm available coverage with your agent. The New York example and insurer descriptions here were checked on October 15, 2026.
</Callout>

---

## Compare the policy terms

Ask the agent to explain the proposal's limits, exclusions and endorsements. Have them show what each recommendation covers in your actual operations.

Bring these questions to the review:

- Who and what does the policy insure, and at which locations?
- When does coverage begin and end?
- What is the deductible, and can the church pay it after a loss?
- What limits apply, and what losses would remain the church's responsibility?
- Which activities or property are excluded?
- How should you notify the insurer about a claim?

Ask for clarification before choosing. Keep the policy documents and the agent's explanations with your insurance records.

---

## Review coverage as the church changes

Review coverage annually and when your operations, property or activities change. Use the review to revisit your inventory and the ministry description you gave the agent.

- [ ] Describe changed activities and meeting locations.
- [ ] Update the equipment list and supporting records.
- [ ] Revisit staffing and transportation arrangements.
- [ ] Compare the policy with current venue requirements.
- [ ] Ask the agent to explain remaining gaps or exclusions.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Commit your works to Yahweh And your plans will be established."* — Proverbs 16:3 (LSB)
</Callout>

title: Church Insurance Basics

sources.claim: Opening; ministry description; compare terms; notification questions. Editorial questions apply the guide to a church plant without asserting specific coverage.

claim_check.notes: Independent Opus review passed 2026-10-15 at a3d936a9ce4efaf111eba882c80f79ad848cb783. The b4b75c7 review checked all 17 sources, Proverbs 16:3 (LSB) and the screenshots, and failed only the abuse-prevention sentence. a3d936a changes only that sentence and source 13's claim. The new sentence asks whether the insurer requires or offers abuse-prevention measures; the live Church Mutual page describes MinistrySafe safeguards and states no requirement, so the question asserts nothing unsupported. Lint, check-seed and desktop/mobile screenshots pass.

rulings: Phase 0 and financial section match the existing financial references; sort order follows the current published entries.
Describe categories and questions only. No premiums, universal liability limits or national workers’ compensation thresholds.
Label New York as an example and refer each reader to the agency governing their own workers.
No new theology, pastoral-care or child-protection methodology. The scripture stands without an insurance-related interpretation.
All volatile coverage descriptions and the state example are as of 2026-10-15; verify current agency requirements and actual policy terms.
